We need to parse the problem: We have a binary array nums (0/1). A subarray is considered good if it contains exactly one element with value 1 (i.e., exactly one 1). Need to find number of ways to split the array into subarrays (contiguous partitions) such that each subarray is good (i.e., each subarray has exactly one '1').

Essentially we need to partition the array into contiguous parts each containing exactly one '1'. The total number of 1's in the array is, say, m. For a valid partition, each part must have exactly one '1', so we need exactly m parts, each containing one 1. The array may also have zeros; these zeros must be assigned to the neighboring parts: i.e., zeros between 1's can be split between the left part (the part containing the previous 1) and right part (the part containing the next 1). Zeros before the first 1 must belong to the first part; zeros after the last 1 must belong to the last part. So the number of ways depends on gaps of zeros between consecutive 1's: each gap of length L (number of zeros between two consecutive 1's) contributes (L+1) ways to decide where to cut between the two parts (i.e., you can place the dividing cut at any point among the L+1 possible positions: after 0 zeros, after 1 zero, ..., after L zeros). Actually think: Suppose we have ...1 [zeros of length L] 1... The first 1 belongs to left subarray, second 1 belongs to right subarray. The subarray of left part ends somewhere among the zeros (including possibly after the first 1 with zero zeros after? Actually left part must contain exactly that left 1 and may include some zeros to its right before the cut). The right part must contain the right 1 and may include some zeros to its left before the cut. The cut must be placed somewhere in between these two ones: you can put the cut after k zeros of the gap, where k ranges from 0 to L (i.e., you can allocate k zeros to the left subarray and L-k zeros to the right subarray). So there are L+1 possibilities.
